title: Impact of YouTube User-Generated Content on News Dissemination and Youth Information Reception
screen_reason: Mixed-methods study whose content-analysis arm coded 200 YouTube news videos and reports item-level shares with a stated denominator: 'misinformation prevalent in 38.0% of analysed videos' (Abstract), 45% of videos rated low credibility and 21% high, and misleading thumbnails in 45% of cases. A share of items in a sample carrying a misinformation label qualifies, so INCLUDE - but with strong reservations recorded below: the misinformation label is never operationalised anywhere in the Methods or Results, the 38.0% appears ONLY in the Abstract, and the credibility variables are quality ratings rather than truth/falsity judgements.

estimates.country: Not stated for the video sample; the study population spans the United States, Brazil, India, China and Japan
estimates.date: Not dated; 'Data were collected over 6 weeks' (article received 21 March 2025, published 2025)
estimates.measure_type: % of analysed YouTube news videos in which misinformation was present
estimates.value_raw: misinformation prevalent in 38.0% of analysed videos (of n = 200)
estimates.denominator: 200 YouTube news videos selected on recent view counts, sharing metrics and topic diversity (politics, health, entertainment, global affairs)
estimates.definition: NOT OPERATIONALISED in the paper. The Methods say only that 'credibility was assessed by referencing official data or journalistic sources' and that framing was coded sensationalist/neutral/analytical; Figure 7b reports 'patterns of misinformation or low-credibility tactics' as lack of proper sourcing, conspiratorial language and misleading thumbnails, i.e. proxies rather than verified falsity.
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition of misinformation is given anywhere in the article; the term is used throughout without a case definition
estimates.source_quote: Sensationalist content attracted higher engagement (30.0%) but had lower credibility, with misinformation prevalent in 38.0% of analysed videos.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results (this figure appears ONLY in the Abstract; the Results section and Figure 7 caption do not repeat it)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two coders evaluated 20% of the videos with Cohen's kappa = 0.82, discrepancies resolved by consensus; coding supported by MAXQDA 2022. Credibility was assessed 'by referencing official data or journalistic sources'. No codebook, no per-variable reliability, and no rule for what makes a video count as containing misinformation.
estimates.moderator_quote: A content analysis of 200 YouTube news videos examined structure, framing and engagement across cultural contexts. Videos were selected based on recent view counts, sharing metrics and topic diversity, including politics, health, entertainment and global affairs. Two coders evaluated 20% of videos (Cohen's kappa = 0.82), resolving discrepancies through consensus. Framing was categorised as sensationalist, neutral, or analytical; credibility was assessed by referencing official data or journalistic sources.
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE and low confidence. The 38.0% is stated only in the Abstract and is never reproduced, decomposed or defined in the Results; the closest Results text gives 45% low credibility, 21% high credibility, 30% sensationalist framing and 45% misleading thumbnails, none of which equals 38%. Because the label 'misinformation' is the authors' own and the coding referent (official data / journalistic sources) is external, I coded this CONTENT rather than QUALITY, but an adjudicator could defensibly re-code it QUALITY given that the reported misinformation 'patterns' (lack of sourcing, conspiratorial language, misleading thumbnails) are all things a wholly true video could display. Video selection is by view count and 'topic diversity' with no sampling frame, no country attribution, no date range and no video list, so the denominator is not reconstructable. denom_scope coded all_media because the corpus spans multiple news topics rather than one issue.

estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY under the ambiguity rule: a deceptive-presentation tactic that an otherwise accurate video can display, so it is not a verified-falsity share. An adjudicator who treats 'misleading thumbnail' as misleading CONTENT would re-code this CONTENT with breadth=misleading. Note the sentence is ambiguous about whether 45% is the share of all 200 videos or of some subset; read here as the share of the sample, consistent with Figure 7b being a prevalence panel. Full sentence: 'Videos with misleading thumbnails used in 45% of cases achieved 15% more engagement, reflecting the persuasive power of visual sensationalism.' Two-column interleaving again, so only the contiguous fragment is quoted.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Not extracted: framing distribution - sensationalist 30.0%, neutral 42.5% (analytical not printed) - framing style, not veracity. (2) Not extracted: the other two Figure 7b misinformation-pattern categories (lack of proper sourcing, conspiratorial language); their percentages are in the figure only and the figure is not in this text file. (3) Not extracted: comment sentiment shares (positive 40%, neutral 35%, negative 25%, the negative example being 'Fake news, misleading content!') - audience sentiment, not a misinformation share. (4) Not extracted: content-type composition (hard news 35%, health/science 25%, soft news 40%) and engagement scores - composition, not misinformation. (5) Not extracted: survey scale means (UGC news frequency 3.21, trust in UGC 3.48, credibility assessment 78.4, algorithmic awareness 3.75, sharing frequency 3.65) - scale means with no share of respondents, so no row per the protocol. The survey contains NO item measuring self-reported exposure to misinformation. (6) SERIOUS RELIABILITY CONCERNS for the adjudicator: the headline 38.0% appears only in the Abstract; the paper never defines misinformation; the video sample has no dates, no countries, no search strategy and no list; the survey n = 100 (20 per country) is described both as 'stratified random sampling' and as recruited via ads and purposive outreach; the qualitative phase reports 120 interviews from 100 youth plus 20 creators alongside 10 focus groups; the study is published in a health-services journal (Health Expectations) with an IRB approval from a university unaffiliated with any listed author. Several internal numbers do not reconcile (45% low credibility vs 38% misinformation vs 45% misleading thumbnails). I would treat every value from this paper as low confidence.

rob.design: Convergent parallel mixed-methods, data collected over 6 weeks (undated). (a) Survey: 40-item questionnaire (demographics 6, UGC engagement 10, trust 8, credibility assessment 10, algorithmic awareness 6), five-point Likert trust/credibility scales adapted from prior instruments, pilot n = 30 (alpha 0.85 trust, 0.80 credibility); n = 100 participants aged 13-35, 20 per country from the US, Brazil, India, China and Japan, described as stratified random sampling with a power analysis, but recruited via online ads, social media, university mailing lists and direct outreach to creators, with eligibility requiring active YouTube news use. (b) Qualitative: 10 focus groups and 120 semi-structured interviews (100 youth, 20 purposively sampled creators), 45-60 min, thematic coding in NVivo 12, two coders with Cohen's kappa. (c) Content analysis: 200 YouTube news videos selected on recent view counts, sharing metrics and topic diversity; two coders double-coded 20% (Cohen's kappa = 0.82); framing coded sensationalist/neutral/analytical, credibility referenced to official data or journalistic sources, engagement metrics coded in MAXQDA 2022. Analysis in R 4.4.2 and Python 3.9 (ANOVA, multivariate regression, EFA, SEM). Ethics: China Southwest Medical University IRB SWM-0098-DS4. Authors' stated limitations: small sample across five countries, cross-sectional design.
